newsitem.title: USA: Agriculture Dept questioned EPA clean air proposal.
newsitem.headline: Agriculture Dept questioned EPA clean air proposal.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department questioned a plan by the Environmental Protection Agency to tighten air quality standards before EPA made its proposal last November, according to papers released Tuesday.
And an Agriculture Department task force of people from the farm sector recommended last month that EPA should not go ahead with its proposed rule to set stricter limits on smog and soot.
"The EPA proposed air quality standards, in our judgment, are not based on adequate scientific evidence, peer review, and interpretation," the task force said.
"Thus, we recommend that it is premature for EPA to change the existing standard," it said.
EPA has said higher clean air standards were needed to prevent thousands of premature deaths from respiratory ailments, especially among children.
In its comments on the controversial proposal, the Agriculture Department (USDA) raised concern about the costs of meeting new standards, especially for small farmers.

"USDA appreciates the difficulties EPA faces in projecting air quality and the costs and benefits of emissions controls in the year 2007," the department said in papers released by the House Commerce Committee.

"However, EPA's inability to estimate the full attainment costs of the 0.08 ppm (parts per million) primary standard raises questions about the incremental benefits of a ... secondary standard," it said.
The department said many small farms could be affected, largely because the costs of inputs such as diesel fuel for farm equipment could go up.

"Production and/or use of many of these inputs could be affected by emissions control programs including fuel that powers farm equipment, electricity, fertilizers, pesticides, and other agricultural chemicals," it said.

Industry groups and communities are fighting the proposed new standard, which must be finalized by July, arguing that complying with the rules could cost billions of dollars with little health benefit.

Releasing the papers Tuesday, House Commerce Committee chairman Rep. Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, said "they show, once again, that serious concerns about the justification and impact of the EPA's new rules exist within the Clinton Administration itself."
